extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, logicians, and computer scientists interested in formalization and computer verification of mathematics; users and developers of Metamath
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for formalizing mathematical theorems and proofs using the Metamath system, addressing issues of rigor, simplicity, proof representation, trust, and interaction with other computer tools. Focuses on how to write, compress, verify, and archive proofs so they are precise and inspectable by humans and machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Make mathematics accessible so non-specialists and intelligent laypersons can follow proofs (Metamath aims to enable this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamath allows peeling apart formulas and definitions layer by layer so every step is available for inspection; computers could give instant feedback about inference steps, enabling hobbyists and programmers to explore and experiment with conjectures. The text argues that informal mathematical language often misleads lay readers, whereas an explicit computer language can improve accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse of previously proved theorems (hierarchical proof building)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use previously proved theorems rather than proving them from primitives repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should build a hierarchy of theorems and definitions to avoid exploding proof size; this permits expressing complex arguments compactly by referencing prior results instead of unfolding everything to axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce definitions to compress complex formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce definitions along the way so very complex formulas can be represented with few symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to introduce definitions can lead to absurdly long formulas (examples cited: Gödel’s theorem needing ~20,000 primitive symbols; Bourbaki’s enormous encoding of 'one'). Well-chosen defined symbols keep expression sizes manageable and make formally verified proofs feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of the metalanguage
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the metalanguage (the language used to describe mathematics) as simple and minimal as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamath treats all mathematical expressions as simple sequences of symbols, devoid of intrinsic meaning. The mathematical content of the metalanguage should be minimal—only what is needed to make inference rules work—so that virtually anyone can understand the basic rules and the verifier remains straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute rigor and explicit precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Express proofs with absolute precision so correctness can be trusted subject to the assumed axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamath requires formal, explicit proofs where every step is checkable. While Gödel shows we cannot prove consistency of axioms from within, Metamath ensures that, given axioms and definitions, derived results follow with mechanical certainty. Developing proofs in Metamath is challenging but prevents even tiny mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit construction and verification of well-formed formulas (wffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff must be explicitly constructed based on rules defining wffs; do not rely on hidden or built-in wff syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike many proof systems with built-in wff recognition, Metamath requires wff construction rules in the database; a single ordinary formal-proof step may correspond to many Metamath steps that make the implicit validity explicit. Section references note how this leads to more detailed proofs but avoids hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of axioms, rules, and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: All axioms, rules, and definitions used must be available for inspection; do not embed hidden or built-in rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Metamath’s knowledge is supplied by the user, any error can only come from the axioms/definitions in the database. This transparency lets users inspect and understand exactly what assumptions underlie each proof and reduces unseen sources of bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the verifier algorithm simple and small to build trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The verification algorithm should be simple enough to be readily understood so users can trust computer-checked proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the core algorithm is small and comprehensible, mathematicians will trust computer verification (analogy to trusting pocket calculators). Independent implementations of the verifier further reduce doubts; the book notes there are many independent Metamath verifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid large, complex proof-verification programs that are bug-prone
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize built-in complexity in proof-verification programs because large programs are harder to understand and more likely to contain bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As more definitions and features are added, verifier programs grow and become harder to manually validate. Metamath’s minimal approach limits verifier complexity, reducing the chance of subtle bugs that would compromise trust in machine-checked proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof conciseness and elegance as a desirable goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for short, elegant proofs—proof length can serve as an objective measure of beauty or elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The set.mm database’s goal was to make proofs as short as possible. Shorter proofs are generally considered more elegant; while Metamath produces many detailed steps, one should also aim to keep proofs concise via definitions and theorem reuse when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate results originating from computer algebra systems (provenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When incorporating results from computer algebra systems into formal proofs, mark their source/provenance explicitly (e.g., add a hypothesis indicating 'maple').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because CAS packages have their own heuristics and possible bugs, adding a provenance hypothesis (like a constant maple) indicates reliance on that system: 'assuming Maple is consistent, then...'. This preserves rigor by making external trust assumptions explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish theorem-proving tools from archival proof systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat automated theorem provers as proof-search tools and use systems like Metamath to archive and verify resulting theorems and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theorem prover typically focuses on finding a single theorem, while Metamath is meant to store both the theorem and its proof in a database for verification and reuse. Automatically generated proofs may be long and should be manually rewritten for concision before being archived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to express different logics and self-referential systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the freedom to define arbitrary wff notation and express varied logical systems, including higher-order logics and self-descriptive constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamath’s minimal built-in syntax allows encoding of first-order, higher-order, modal, intuitionist, and other logical systems; with suitable axioms and definitions one can even express and reason about Metamath itself (reflection principles). This flexibility is a design goal but requires careful database design.
